Awaiting Placement
Steps · Gap · MA share · Calculator · Both sides · Methods

Ready to leave the hospital. Still waiting for the next bed.

When a hospital patient on a Medicare Advantage plan needs rehab or a skilled nursing facility next, the move can wait on the plan's approval. Those extra days add up to beds.

No. 01

The last step before leaving

A patient is awaiting placement when they are medically ready to leave the hospital but cannot safely go home. They need a bed somewhere that can keep caring for them: a skilled nursing facility, an inpatient rehabilitation facility, or a long-term care hospital. Until that bed is arranged, they stay in a hospital bed.

Arranging the move takes several handoffs, and any of them can add a day. A facility may not have a bed, a family may need time to choose, or a request may be missing information. Coverage shapes two steps. Medicare Advantage (MA) plans can limit which facilities are in network, and they can require their approval, called prior authorization, before a patient moves to a facility. If the plan denies the request, the hospital can ask for a peer-to-peer review with the plan's physician, appeal, or look for a different level of care. Traditional Medicare does not require prior authorization for these stays. It pays for a skilled nursing stay only after three inpatient midnights, and observation days do not count, though most MA plans and many accountable care organizations waive that rule. Some patients no longer need skilled care at all and wait for a custodial placement that neither program pays for.

  1. 1Medically readyThe care team agrees the patient no longer needs hospital care.
  2. 2Referral sentA case manager sends referrals to facilities that can meet the patient's needs.
  3. 3Facility acceptsA facility reviews the record and offers a bed.
  4. 4Plan authorizationMA plans can require it. Traditional Medicare does not for these stays.
  5. 5Transport home or to facilityThe hospital bed opens for the next patient.

Where patients go next

  • Home
  • Home health
  • Skilled nursing
  • Inpatient rehab
  • Long-term care hospital

Since Jan 2026 For items and services subject to prior authorization, impacted payers, including MA plans, must now send standard decisions within seven calendar days instead of 14. The 72-hour deadline for expedited requests already applied. MA plans may extend a standard decision by up to 14 calendar days in some cases, such as when the enrollee asks for it. No. 02

How much longer

On average, Medicare Advantage (MA) patients stay in the hospital longer than traditional Medicare patients. The gap is small for patients who go home and widens for those who need a facility next. These figures come from MedPAC, the commission that advises Congress on Medicare payment.

Where patients went next also differs by coverage: MA patients were more likely than traditional Medicare patients to leave the hospital without post-acute care.

For the few patients who go on to a long-term care hospital, the median hospital stay was 13 days in traditional Medicare and 21 days in Medicare Advantage (2023, unadjusted). (MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab))

What this gap does and does not show

  • The averages above are unadjusted. After MedPAC adjusts for hospital, diagnosis group and destination, the gap by destination is smaller (for inpatient rehab, 2.3 days instead of 2.9). (MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab))
  • MA patients had a higher risk of observation stays for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions than traditional Medicare patients (relative risk 2.38). (Beckman et al., Potentially avoidable acute care use, MA vs traditional Medicare, JAMA Health Forum 2023 (opens in a new tab))
  • MA and traditional Medicare enrollees in MedPAC's 2023 sample differed: 27 percent of MA enrollees and 17 percent of traditional Medicare beneficiaries were dually eligible or received the low-income subsidy. (MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab))
  • MA plans told MedPAC that prior authorization helps ensure beneficiaries get to the right level of care, and some delays come from incomplete information in the request. (MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab))

No. 03

A growing share of the room

In the hospitals studied here, Medicare Advantage (MA) rose from 29% of Medicare discharges in FY2016 to 53% in FY2024. Over the same years, average stays rose for both MA and traditional Medicare patients.

For context, KFF reports that 55% of Medicare beneficiaries were enrolled in MA in 2026. That counts people, not hospital discharges. (KFF, Medicare Advantage in 2026: Enrollment Update and Key Trends (opens in a new tab))

Look up a hospital

Each hospital has its own stay gap and MA share. Search by name, city or six-digit CMS certification number (CCN).

    The waiting room calculator

    Start from a typical hospital or look one up by name, then move the share of Medicare patients in Medicare Advantage (MA) plans. The calculator multiplies the hospital's MA discharges by the extra days MedPAC measured for each discharge destination. It shows the result as beds held on an average day.

    Every result is an estimate built from national averages and the inputs shown. The gaps are associations: they do not show what causes the longer stays.

      • Current authorization waitDefault: 2.5 days

        Set from the AMRPA survey average of just over 2.5 days for inpatient rehabilitation decisions. The survey did not measure skilled nursing facilities. The model applies the same wait to both, which is an assumption.

        Source: AMRPA, 2024 Medicare Advantage prior authorization survey (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      • Faster authorization waitDefault: 1.0 day

        An illustrative scenario, not a forecast. Rules allow up to 72 hours for expedited and seven calendar days for standard MA decisions. The AHIP pledge aims for real-time answers to most electronic approvals in 2027.

        Source: eCFR, 42 CFR 422.568, standard organization determination timeframes (opens in a new tab) · government; eCFR, 42 CFR 422.572, expedited organization determination timeframes (opens in a new tab) · government; AHIP, Health Plans Take Action to Simplify Prior Authorization (Jun. 23, 2025) (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      • Variable cost of one extra dayDefault: $800

        About a quarter of KFF's $3,297 expense per adjusted inpatient day (2024, from the AHA Annual Survey), on the reasoning that most staffing, overhead and capital costs do not change with one more low-acuity day. One academic center study found the last full day of a stay cost $420 in 1990s dollars, or 2.4 percent of total stay cost. MedPAC says some hospital costs are fixed and do not rise with a longer stay.

        Source: KFF State Health Facts, Hospital Expenses per Adjusted Inpatient Day (2024: $3,297.26) (opens in a new tab) · nonprofit; Taheri et al., Length of stay has minimal impact on the cost of hospital admission, J Am Coll Surg 2000 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed; MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Per-diem rate (per-diem payment only)Default: $2,500

        Illustrative. No source gives a typical rate. MedPAC reports that MA plans commonly pay critical access hospitals a per diem.

        Source: MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Contribution margin per added admissionDefault: $4,500

        Illustrative. A single figure from a Kaufman Hall example reported by Becker's: an average $4,500 margin per admission for a 425-bed hospital. It is not a national benchmark.

        Source: Becker's Hospital Review, The cost of unnecessary hospital days in 8 numbers (May 14, 2024), citing Kaufman Hall (opens in a new tab) · industry

      • Share of freed bed-days refilledDefault: Set from occupancy, 0 to 100%

        An assumption: the share rises from 0% at 70% occupancy to 100% at 90%. National staffed-bed occupancy was 75.3% in the year after the public health emergency, and 85% is a shortage threshold in the Leuchter model. In a hospital benchmarking study, boarding exceeded 4 hours in 88.9% of hospital-months when occupancy passed 85%. Median occupancy in the FY2024 cost reports is 58.3%, which suggests available beds exceed staffed beds. Override this if your hospital routinely turns patients away.

        Source: Leuchter et al., Health Care Staffing Shortages and Potential National Hospital Bed Shortage, JAMA Netw Open 2025 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed; Janke et al., Hospital Occupancy and Emergency Department Boarding During the COVID-19 Pandemic, JAMA Netw Open 2022 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed; CMS, Cost Reports (HCRIS), hospital form CMS-2552-10 (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Where MA patients go after dischargeDefault: Home 65%, home health 17%, skilled nursing 15%, inpatient rehabilitation 3%

        From MedPAC's 2023 data: 65, 17 and 15 percent for home, home health and skilled nursing, and 3 percent for inpatient rehabilitation (5 percent in traditional Medicare). MedPAC shows long-term care hospitals separately, at under 1 percent of MA discharges, and the model leaves them out.

        Source: MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Which gap counts as extra daysDefault: Placement-related

        Unadjusted and adjusted gaps by discharge destination come from MedPAC Table 4-1. The placement lens is the adjusted gap minus the adjusted gap for patients discharged home, so it shows the extra stay length associated with post-acute placement. MedPAC describes these gaps as associations and says they suggest that plans could slow discharges through activities such as prior authorization.

        Source: MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      No. 05

      Both sides of the counter

      Hospitals point to prior authorization as a cause of discharge delays. Medicare Advantage (MA) plans told MedPAC that it helps ensure beneficiaries get to the right level of care. Each column groups findings by the side that usually cites them, and every item names its source and the type of organization behind it.

      What hospitals point to

      • MedPAC reports that MA plans commonly pay inpatient hospitals per stay by MS-DRG, so a longer stay does not typically bring extra payment.

        MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • In a 2024 survey of 367 inpatient rehabilitation facilities, the average wait for an initial MA prior authorization decision was just over 2.5 days.

        AMRPA, the inpatient rehab trade group, 2024 Medicare Advantage prior authorization survey (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      • In a Florida Hospital Association survey of 95 hospitals, prior authorization was the most common driver of discharge delays, at 40 percent.

        Florida Hospital Association, 2025 Days Awaiting Discharge Survey (fact sheet) (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      • KFF, using OIG data from June 2024, reports MA initial prior authorization denial rates of 65 percent for long-term care hospitals, 54 percent for inpatient rehabilitation facilities and 12 percent for skilled nursing facilities.

        KFF, MA insurers deny prior authorization requests for post-acute care at higher rates (Jul. 6, 2026) (opens in a new tab) · nonprofit

      • An OIG review of 250 sampled prior authorization denials from 15 large MA organizations (June 1 to 7, 2019) estimated that 13 percent of the denied requests met Medicare coverage rules and would likely have been approved under traditional Medicare.

        HHS OIG, OEI-09-18-00260, MA organization denials of prior authorization requests (2022) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • From 2017 to 2023, MA admissions became 1.2 percentage points more likely than traditional Medicare admissions to last 14 or more days. The authors estimated 1.8 million additional bed-days from prolonged MA stays in 2022.

        McGarry et al., Extended Hospital Stays in MA and Traditional Medicare, JAMA Intern Med 2025 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed

      What plans point to

      • MA plans told MedPAC that prior authorization helps ensure beneficiaries get to the right level of care.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • MA plans told MedPAC that some delays come from incomplete information in the request.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Using 2018 claims, a 2023 study found MA enrollees were 6 percent less likely than traditional Medicare patients to be hospitalized for conditions that good outpatient care can often prevent (relative risk 0.94). Plans argue that if fewer of their healthier members are admitted, the MA patients who are admitted may be sicker, and stay longer for reasons other than delay.

        Beckman et al., Potentially avoidable acute care use, MA vs traditional Medicare, JAMA Health Forum 2023 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed

      • MA enrollees used inpatient rehabilitation at about a third of the traditional Medicare rate (5 vs 14 stays per 1,000 in 2023). The MA patients who do go to rehab are a narrower group, so part of their longer hospital stay may reflect who they are, which adjustment for diagnosis group cannot fully remove.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Where a plan pays a hospital by the day, a longer stay is paid for. MedPAC notes most plans pay per stay, but per-diem contracts exist, and under them a hospital has less reason to shorten the stay.

        MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • MedPAC notes that higher use of post-acute care in traditional Medicare may indicate unnecessary care.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Plans that signed the 2025 AHIP pledge committed that, in 2027, at least 80 percent of electronic prior authorization approvals with complete documentation will be answered in real time.

        AHIP, the health plans' trade group, Health Plans Take Action to Simplify Prior Authorization (Jun. 23, 2025) (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      What the evidence can't settle yet

      • MedPAC says lower MA use of post-acute care may indicate efficient care or worse access, and that appropriateness cannot be judged without medical record review.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • MA and traditional Medicare enrollees in MedPAC's 2023 sample differed: 27 percent of MA enrollees and 17 percent of traditional Medicare beneficiaries were dually eligible or received the low-income subsidy.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • When skilled nursing facility denials were appealed, 95 percent were approved. KFF says this raises questions about routine inappropriate denials, and also that insurers may reverse denials to avoid an independent review.

        KFF, MA insurers deny prior authorization requests for post-acute care at higher rates (Jul. 6, 2026) (opens in a new tab) · nonprofit

      • MA patients had a higher risk of observation stays for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions than traditional Medicare patients (relative risk 2.38).

        Beckman et al., Potentially avoidable acute care use, MA vs traditional Medicare, JAMA Health Forum 2023 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed

      Policy timeline

      Rules, reports and commitments on prior authorization, oldest first.

      DateRule or reportSource

      1. Jan 1, 2024

        CMS-4201-F applies

        The final rule (88 FR 22120) applies to coverage beginning January 1, 2024. MA plans must follow traditional Medicare coverage criteria. These include the inpatient admission payment criteria at 42 CFR 412.3 and the coverage criteria for skilled nursing, home health and inpatient rehabilitation.

        Federal Register, CMS-4201-F, Contract Year 2024 Policy and Technical Changes (88 FR 22120) (opens in a new tab) · government; eCFR, 42 CFR 422.101, requirements relating to basic benefits (opens in a new tab) · government

      2. Oct 17, 2024

        Senate subcommittee majority staff report

        The majority staff of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations reported that UnitedHealthcare, Humana and CVS denied post-acute care prior authorization requests at higher rates than other care in 2022. UnitedHealthcare's initial denial rate for skilled nursing facility requests rose from 1.4 percent in 2019 to 12.6 percent in 2022.

        U.S. Senate PSI, Refusal of Recovery (majority staff), Oct. 17, 2024 (opens in a new tab) · government

      3. Jun 23, 2025

        Insurer prior authorization pledge

        Health plans, through AHIP, committed to six actions on prior authorization, covering commercial, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care coverage. The commitments are voluntary. CMS and HHS announced the pledge the same day.

        AHIP, Health Plans Take Action to Simplify Prior Authorization (Jun. 23, 2025) (opens in a new tab) · trade group; CMS, HHS and CMS secure industry pledge on prior authorization (Jun. 23, 2025) (opens in a new tab) · government

      4. Jan 1, 2026

        CMS-0057-F shorter standard deadline begins

        For items and services subject to prior authorization, impacted payers, including MA plans, must now send standard decisions within seven calendar days instead of 14. The 72-hour deadline for expedited requests already applied. MA plans may extend a standard decision by up to 14 calendar days in some cases, such as when the enrollee asks for it.

        CMS, Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) fact sheet (opens in a new tab) · government; eCFR, 42 CFR 422.568, standard organization determination timeframes (opens in a new tab) · government; eCFR, 42 CFR 422.572, expedited organization determination timeframes (opens in a new tab) · government

      5. Jun 2026

        MedPAC June 2026 report, Chapter 4

        MedPAC reported that MA stays averaged about 5.7 days against 5.2 for traditional Medicare in FY2024. After adjustment, the gap was 11.2 percent overall and 32.3 percent for stays ending in an inpatient rehabilitation facility.

        MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      6. Jul 6, 2026

        KFF summarizes OIG post-acute denial findings

        KFF reported OIG findings from June 2024 data: initial denials of 65 percent for long-term care hospitals, 54 percent for inpatient rehabilitation facilities and 12 percent for skilled nursing facilities.

        KFF, MA insurers deny prior authorization requests for post-acute care at higher rates (Jul. 6, 2026) (opens in a new tab) · nonprofit

      7. Sep 4, 2026

        MedPAC post-acute care session

        MedPAC staff presented preliminary 2023 data. Median hospital stays were longer for MA enrollees at every discharge destination, and MA enrollees were discharged less often to skilled nursing, rehabilitation and long-term care hospitals.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      8. Jan 1, 2027 Upcoming

        API requirements and pledge targets

        Impacted payers generally have until January 1, 2027 to meet the CMS-0057-F API requirements, including a Prior Authorization API. The AHIP pledge sets the same date for a standardized electronic prior authorization framework.

        CMS, Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) fact sheet (opens in a new tab) · government; AHIP, Health Plans Take Action to Simplify Prior Authorization (Jun. 23, 2025) (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      Hospital figures from cost reports

      Hospitals that bill Medicare file a cost report each year. This site reads the FY2016 to FY2024 reports for counts of days and discharges by payer, from CMS's HCRIS hospital files (form CMS-2552-10). Each raw file is pinned by its SHA-256 hash in pipeline/sources.json in the public code, so a rebuild reads the same bytes; CMS refreshes these files quarterly, so a fresh download can differ.

      Definitions

      Fiscal year
      The federal fiscal year the report period begins in, which is how CMS files the reports. When a hospital has more than one report for a year, the longest period is kept, then the most recently processed. FY2024 reports begin between Oct 2023 and Sep 2024, so the latest run to Sep 2025. MedPAC's FY2024 figures cover discharges from Oct 2023 to Sep 2024.
      Report length
      Reports must cover at least 300 days. Counts from a report longer than 366 days are scaled to 365 days on hospital pages and in the calculator (7 in FY2024); stays and shares are ratios and need no scaling. Reports of every status (as submitted, settled, reopened or amended) are used.
      Medicare Advantage (MA) days and discharges
      Worksheet S-3, Part I, line 2 (labeled "HMO and other" on the form): days in column 6, discharges in column 13.
      Traditional Medicare days
      Line 1 plus lines 8 to 12 (intensive care and other special-care units, including any subscripted unit lines such as 8.01), column 6. Line 2 counts MA days in every unit, so the special-care lines are added to traditional Medicare to compare like with like. Traditional Medicare is the fee-for-service (FFS) program. Where a Pennsylvania Rural Health Model hospital splits its Medicare days between columns 6 and 6.01, the two are added.
      Traditional Medicare discharges
      Line 1, column 13.
      Total discharges
      Line 1, column 15, all payers.
      Average stay and gap
      Days divided by discharges, for each group. The gap is the MA average minus the traditional Medicare average.
      MA share
      MA discharges divided by MA plus traditional Medicare discharges.
      Beds and occupancy
      Beds and available bed-days from line 14, columns 2 and 3. Occupancy is inpatient days (line 14, column 8, minus nursery days on line 13) divided by available bed-days. At hospitals with swing beds, line 14's inpatient days include swing-bed days (lines 5 and 6), so their occupancy can read high. A value above 100% or below 5% is flagged and not shown.
      Teaching hospital
      At least 10 full-time-equivalent interns and residents (line 14, column 9), shown as a badge on hospital pages. The Academic preset counts any reported resident.
      Names and cities
      CMS Hospital General Information, matched by CMS certification number (CCN). The cost-report name is used when there is no match.

      Which hospitals are included

      Short-term acute care hospitals only: those whose CCN ends in 0001 to 0879. Critical access hospitals use a different range (1300 to 1399) and are not included. Each FY2024 report is checked against the rules below in order and counted under the first rule it fails. The CCN range also takes in some specialty hospitals, such as PPS-exempt cancer hospitals, when their reports pass.

      RuleExcluded, FY2024
      In Puerto Rico, or in Maryland (Maryland hospitals are not paid under the national inpatient payment system)96
      Report covers fewer than 300 days98
      No MA discharges reported236

      6 hospitals whose gap is larger than 3 days either way, or whose MA and traditional Medicare stays differ more than twofold, are kept but marked "check this hospital's data" on their page; the calculator uses national averages for them.

      The national trend on the main page applies the same rules to each year from FY2016 to FY2024. The COVID years, FY2020 to FY2022, are shaded. National figures pool the included hospitals: total MA days divided by total MA discharges, and likewise for traditional Medicare and for the MA share, so each hospital counts in proportion to its discharges. The hospitals that pass the checks change from year to year (2,700 in FY2016, 2,563 in FY2024), so part of a trend can be a change in which hospitals are counted.

      Cross-check

      Weighted by discharges, the included FY2024 reports give an average MA stay of 5.67 days and a traditional Medicare stay of 5.18 days. MedPAC's claims-based figures for FY2024 are 5.7 and 5.2 days. The largest difference is 0.03 days. (MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab))

      What the cost-report figures can't show

      • The gap is raw. It is not adjusted for diagnosis or severity, and cost reports do not say where patients went after discharge.
      • Across the 2,563 hospitals with both figures, the gap does not rise with MA share (correlation of −0.16). Where nearly all Medicare patients are in MA, the few left in traditional Medicare are a small, selected group, so their average is less stable.
      • Hospitals file these reports themselves, and a few figures are implausible. Occupancy outside 5% to 100% is flagged and not shown (9 hospitals in FY2024).
      • 236 FY2024 reports show no MA discharges at all. That is more likely a gap in reporting than a hospital with no MA patients; those reports are excluded, as the table above shows.

      The calculator

      The calculator estimates how many beds a hospital's MA patients hold on an average day because their stays run longer. It applies MedPAC's national gaps by discharge destination to one hospital's volumes. It is a model built on averages, not a measurement of any hospital. "Extra days" here means the difference between MA and traditional Medicare stays. It is not the same as days over the DRG's expected length of stay or as avoidable days logged by case managers.

      Extra days per MA stay

      DestinationShare of MA patientsUnadjustedAdjustedPlacement-related
      Home65%0.30.20.0
      Home health17%0.50.40.2
      Skilled nursing15%1.61.41.2
      Inpatient rehab3.0%2.92.32.1
      • Unadjusted and adjusted gaps are MedPAC's, for FY2024. The adjustment accounts for the hospital, the diagnosis group (MS-DRG) and the discharge destination. (MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab))
      • Placement-related is the adjusted gap minus the adjusted gap for patients who went home on their own (0.2 days). It keeps only the extra days associated with going to post-acute care, and it is the default.
      • This hospital's own gap, offered once a hospital is chosen, scales the adjusted column so that its average across the mix equals the hospital's cost-report gap. A gap of zero or less counts as no extra days.
      • The mix is MedPAC's for 2023. MedPAC reports that 3% of MA hospital discharges go to inpatient rehab (5% in traditional Medicare), and the model uses that share. Long-term care hospitals are shown separately, at about 0.5% of MA stays, and are left out. (MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab))

      Formulas

      In these formulas, d is a destination, mix[d] the share of MA patients who go there and e[d] the extra days per stay under the chosen gap. t0 and t1 are the plan decision times today and with faster decisions. cvar is the variable cost of a day, rate the per-diem rate and cm the margin on an added admission.

      MA discharges
      nMA = discharges × Medicare share × MA share
      Average stay, all patients
      alos = occupancy × beds × 365 / discharges
      Extra MA bed-days a year
      W = nMA × Σ mix[d] × e[d]
      Beds held on an average day
      E = W / 365
      Share of beds
      E / beds
      Days added to the average stay
      W / discharges
      Occupancy without the extra MA days
      occupancy − W / (beds × 365)
      Speed-up, skilled nursing and inpatient rehab only
      s = max(0, t0 − t1)
      Bed-days freed, summed over skilled nursing and inpatient rehab
      S = nMA × Σ mix[d] × min(s, e[d])
      Added admissions
      A = S × fill / alos
      Refill share, unless set by hand
      fill = min(1, max(0, (occupancy − 0.70) / 0.20))
      Per case: net on the extra days
      −W × cvar
      Per case: net from faster decisions
      S × cvar + A × cm
      Per diem: net on the extra days
      W × (rate − cvar)
      Per diem: net from faster decisions
      A × cm − S × (rate − cvar)

      W is capped at the hospital's occupied bed-days (occupancy × beds × 365), and S cannot exceed W. Every input is held to the range below, so a typed or linked value outside it is moved to the nearest limit.

      Assumptions

      • Current authorization waitDefault: 2.5 days

        Set from the AMRPA survey average of just over 2.5 days for inpatient rehabilitation decisions. The survey did not measure skilled nursing facilities. The model applies the same wait to both, which is an assumption.

        AMRPA, 2024 Medicare Advantage prior authorization survey (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      • Faster authorization waitDefault: 1.0 day

        An illustrative scenario, not a forecast. Rules allow up to 72 hours for expedited and seven calendar days for standard MA decisions. The AHIP pledge aims for real-time answers to most electronic approvals in 2027.

        eCFR, 42 CFR 422.568, standard organization determination timeframes (opens in a new tab) · government; eCFR, 42 CFR 422.572, expedited organization determination timeframes (opens in a new tab) · government; AHIP, Health Plans Take Action to Simplify Prior Authorization (Jun. 23, 2025) (opens in a new tab) · trade group

      • Variable cost of one extra dayDefault: $800

        About a quarter of KFF's $3,297 expense per adjusted inpatient day (2024, from the AHA Annual Survey), on the reasoning that most staffing, overhead and capital costs do not change with one more low-acuity day. One academic center study found the last full day of a stay cost $420 in 1990s dollars, or 2.4 percent of total stay cost. MedPAC says some hospital costs are fixed and do not rise with a longer stay.

        KFF State Health Facts, Hospital Expenses per Adjusted Inpatient Day (2024: $3,297.26) (opens in a new tab) · nonprofit; Taheri et al., Length of stay has minimal impact on the cost of hospital admission, J Am Coll Surg 2000 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed; MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Per-diem rate (per-diem payment only)Default: $2,500

        Illustrative. No source gives a typical rate. MedPAC reports that MA plans commonly pay critical access hospitals a per diem.

        MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Contribution margin per added admissionDefault: $4,500

        Illustrative. A single figure from a Kaufman Hall example reported by Becker's: an average $4,500 margin per admission for a 425-bed hospital. It is not a national benchmark.

        Becker's Hospital Review, The cost of unnecessary hospital days in 8 numbers (May 14, 2024), citing Kaufman Hall (opens in a new tab) · industry

      • Share of freed bed-days refilledDefault: Set from occupancy, 0 to 100%

        An assumption: the share rises from 0% at 70% occupancy to 100% at 90%. National staffed-bed occupancy was 75.3% in the year after the public health emergency, and 85% is a shortage threshold in the Leuchter model. In a hospital benchmarking study, boarding exceeded 4 hours in 88.9% of hospital-months when occupancy passed 85%. Median occupancy in the FY2024 cost reports is 58.3%, which suggests available beds exceed staffed beds. Override this if your hospital routinely turns patients away.

        Leuchter et al., Health Care Staffing Shortages and Potential National Hospital Bed Shortage, JAMA Netw Open 2025 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed; Janke et al., Hospital Occupancy and Emergency Department Boarding During the COVID-19 Pandemic, JAMA Netw Open 2022 (opens in a new tab) · peer-reviewed; CMS, Cost Reports (HCRIS), hospital form CMS-2552-10 (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Where MA patients go after dischargeDefault: Home 65%, home health 17%, skilled nursing 15%, inpatient rehabilitation 3%

        From MedPAC's 2023 data: 65, 17 and 15 percent for home, home health and skilled nursing, and 3 percent for inpatient rehabilitation (5 percent in traditional Medicare). MedPAC shows long-term care hospitals separately, at under 1 percent of MA discharges, and the model leaves them out.

        MedPAC, post-acute care use in traditional Medicare and MA, staff slides, Sept. 4, 2026 (preliminary) (opens in a new tab) · government

      • Which gap counts as extra daysDefault: Placement-related

        Unadjusted and adjusted gaps by discharge destination come from MedPAC Table 4-1. The placement lens is the adjusted gap minus the adjusted gap for patients discharged home, so it shows the extra stay length associated with post-acute placement. MedPAC describes these gaps as associations and says they suggest that plans could slow discharges through activities such as prior authorization.

        MedPAC, Report to the Congress, June 2026, Ch. 4 (Table 4-1, FY 2024 MedPAR) (opens in a new tab) · government

      What the calculator does not measure

      • The share of extra days that were truly avoidable. MedPAC's gaps are associations and do not answer that.
      • Decision times for skilled nursing facilities. The default wait comes from a survey of inpatient rehabilitation facilities, and the model applies it to both.
      • How many MA contracts pay hospitals per diem rather than per case. MedPAC says per-stay payment is common; the per-diem option is there for contracts that differ.

      The national estimate

      MedPAC counted 207 acute hospital stays per 1,000 MA enrollees in 2023, in a sample of 27.8 million enrollees: about 5,754,600 stays. Applying the mix and the extra days per stay gives 1,594,024 extra MA bed-days a year under the placement-related gap (4,367 beds on an average day) and 2,744,944 under the full adjusted gap (7,520 beds). It combines 2023 volumes with FY2024 gaps, so read it as a rough range.

      Limitations

      • These are associations, not causes. Neither MedPAC's gaps nor the cost-report gaps show why MA stays run longer. Prior authorization is one possible reason among several.
      • MedPAC's adjustment accounts for hospital, diagnosis group and destination, but not for every difference between patients. Income and dual eligibility, for example, differ between the two groups.
      • Observation stays are outpatient and are not in these counts. MA patients are more likely to have observation stays for some conditions, which can change who is counted as an inpatient.
      • The calculator applies national averages to one hospital. A hospital's own patients, contracts and post-acute options will differ.
      • Dollar figures rest on single illustrative inputs. They are not a hospital's finances.
      • MedPAC's September 2026 figures, used for the discharge mix and median stays, are preliminary.
